content: Improved training and quality assurance systems are essential to address the limitations of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Despite their limitations, RDTs often remain the only feasible option for infectious disease screening in resource-limited settings. Therefore, further research and the development of specific guidelines for the use of RDTs in blood safety and patient screening are urgently needed. To enhance global adoption, it is critical to reduce the costs of these assays and ensure their ease of use across diverse endemic settings. Many countries worldwide cannot afford high-quality laboratory-based testing, such as enzyme immunoassays (EIAs), and the use of nucleic acid testing (NAT) to minimize the infection window period and detect occult hepatitis remains inaccessible in many regions. Meta-analyses and other studies suggest that assays for detecting hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), including RDTs and EIAs, have significant potential to contribute to the global control of hepatitis B, particularly in endemic areas, which are often resource-constrained and remote. RDTs offer additional advantages, such as easy storage, minimal sample volume requirements, and reduced need for staff training or specialized equipment. However, current challenges include poor clinical and analytical sensitivity, as well as difficulties in detecting occult hepatitis B and mutant variants, leading to missed cases. Sensitivity is also notably reduced in HIV-positive patients, raising further concerns. Conducting systematic reviews of in vitro diagnostic performance in resource-limited settings is challenging due to significant variability in study quality and frequent omission of key parameters. Promoting adherence to globally accepted standards for conducting and reporting diagnostic accuracy studies can improve the current evidence base. High-quality studies are urgently needed to evaluate the accuracy of RDTs in various settings and to support the growing body of evidence. Specifically, research focusing on the impact of geographic variations and mutant phenotypes would be invaluable. The included studies demonstrate excellent specificity across all assays, which is reassuring for cost-effective implementation of diagnostic algorithms for further investigation and treatment. The ease of use of RDTs at all levels of the healthcare system is another significant advantage. The weighting of factors such as cost, ease of use, and diagnostic accuracy is country-specific and could be modeled to optimize implementation strategies.
